items.prompt: What is 'framing', as defined in L1?
choices: Choosing which true facts to emphasize, and in what order, without omitting anything material or asserting anything false
Presenting information in whatever order events actually happened
Selectively hiding negative facts to make an outcome look better
Adding persuasive but false details to strengthen a narrative
items.explanation: Framing is specifically about emphasis and order among true, complete facts — not omission (that's spin) or fabrication (that's lying).
items.reference:
Framing
✅ All facts true
✅ Nothing material omitted
Why: this is what separates legitimate narrative choice from spin or lying.
items.learnMore:
Framing: what it changes, what it doesn't

Framing works only on how true facts are presented — never on the facts themselves.

ChangesOrder, emphasis, lead position
Never changesWhich facts exist, or their truth value

A framed narrative and its driest, most literal retelling agree on every checkable claim — they just don't feel the same to read.

Common mistake

Treating any deliberate ordering as manipulation. Deliberate framing of true, complete facts is just good communication — the ethical line sits at omission and falsehood, not at having a point of view.

items.prompt: According to L1, does framing require changing any facts?
choices: No — the facts underneath stay identical either way
Yes — framing always requires adjusting at least one fact slightly
Yes, but only facts that are negative
L1 doesn't address whether framing changes facts
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that framing changes emphasis and order, not the underlying facts — the same set of true facts can be told multiple ways.
items.reference:

✅ All facts true
✅ Nothing material omitted
Why: this is what separates legitimate narrative choice from spin or lying.

items.prompt: What is 'emphasis', as defined in L1?

Whether a fact is delivered verbally or in writing
items.explanation: Emphasis is specifically about space and prominence within a narrative — independent of formatting choices like bold text or delivery medium.
items.reference:

📏 Space devoted to a fact
Why: emphasis is independent of whether a fact is positive or negative.
items.learnMore:
Emphasis: the three levers
LeverWhat it does
Lead positionWhat's read or heard first
SpaceHow many words or sentences a fact gets
SpecificityA vague gesture vs. a named detail

Common mistake

items.prompt: What is 'spin', as defined in L1?
choices: Presenting true individual facts in a way that omits material context, creating a misleading overall impression
Any narrative that emphasizes positive facts over negative ones
Stating something that is factually false
Presenting facts in chronological order
items.explanation: Spin is specifically about material omission creating a misleading impression, even though every individual statement remains true — distinct from both framing and lying.
items.reference:
Spin
✅ Every sentence checks out true
🚫 Material fact missing entirely
Why: the tell is in what's missing, not in any single sentence.
items.learnMore:
Why spin survives a fact-check

A fact-checker who reads a spun narrative sentence by sentence finds nothing to flag — every individual claim is accurate.

CheckSpin's result
Any false sentence?No
Any material fact missing?Yes

That's exactly why spin is the harder case: catching it means comparing the narrative to what's absent, not to what's present.

Common mistake

Assuming a clean fact-check means a narrative is automatically honest. Passing the truth check is necessary, not sufficient — materiality is a second, independent check.

L1 states spin and lying are equally easy to identify
items.explanation: L1 explains this exact difficulty — spin's individual sentences all check out as true, so the problem only becomes visible by checking for what's absent.

items.prompt: What is 'narrative ownership', as defined in L1?
choices: Proactively telling the story of your own work yourself, rather than leaving it to be assembled secondhand
Legally claiming credit for a project's outcome regardless of who did the work
Refusing to let anyone else discuss your project
Writing a project's documentation before the project is finished
items.explanation: Narrative ownership is specifically about proactively telling your own story, rather than a legal claim or a restriction on others discussing the work.
items.reference:
Narrative ownership
🗣️ Tell it yourself, proactively
🔀 Not assembled secondhand
Why: the alternative to owning the story is someone else's version filling the gap.
items.learnMore:
What fills the silence

If you don't tell the story of your own work, someone else's first impression becomes the default version — and first impressions are rarely complete.

You own itThe reader gets your deliberate, complete account
You don'tThe reader assembles it from rumor, a partial fact, or whoever talked first

Narrative ownership isn't about controlling what other people are allowed to say — it's about not leaving a vacuum for an incomplete version to fill first.

Common mistake

Confusing narrative ownership with spin. Owning the story only works if what you tell is the same true, complete account from L1's framing definition — telling your story first doesn't license telling a misleading one.

items.prompt: According to L2, what is the test for whether an omitted fact makes a narrative spin?
choices: Whether a reasonable reader's understanding of the outcome would actually change if they learned the fact
Whether the fact was mentioned in any prior conversation
Whether the fact is longer than one sentence to explain
Whether the fact happened before or after the project's official end date
items.explanation: L2 defines materiality specifically as whether a reasonable reader's understanding would change — not sentence length, timing, or prior mentions.
items.reference:
Materiality
❓ Would the reader's understanding change?
Why: not "everything" — just what actually changes the picture.
items.learnMore:
Materiality: the one question that matters

Not every omitted detail is spin — only omitting a fact that would change a reasonable reader's understanding of the outcome counts.

DetailMaterial?
Which IDE the team usedNo
The project shipped 3 weeks lateYes
The specific brand of coffee in the break roomNo
A 12-minute outage occurredYes

The test isn't length, timing, or how embarrassing a fact is — it's whether leaving it out would let a reasonable reader walk away with a wrong picture of what happened.

Common mistake

Using 'I could justify leaving it out' as the test. The real test is the reader's resulting understanding, not the writer's ability to rationalize an omission after the fact.

L2 doesn't address whether every detail must be included

items.prompt: According to L2, is reporting facts in strict chronological order a 'neutral' way to avoid the risks of framing?
choices: No — chronological order isn't neutral either; it just means someone else's instinctive reaction becomes the default framing
Yes — chronological order is the only truly neutral way to present facts
Yes, but only for updates shorter than one paragraph

items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects the idea that chronological order is neutral — not choosing a deliberate framing just hands the framing decision to instinct or convention instead.
items.reference:
Why avoiding framing doesn't work
🎲 No deliberate order ≠ neutral
📖 The reader's assumptions fill the gap
Why: owning the narrative honestly is the alternative to an undeliberate default, not a departure from honesty.
items.learnMore:
Why 'just be chronological' doesn't dodge the choice

Chronological order looks neutral because no one appears to have decided it — but "first we failed, then we fixed it" and "we delivered the result, after a failure we fixed" are both chronological, and they don't read the same.

ChoiceWhat fills the gap
Deliberate framingThe writer's considered judgment about order and emphasis
Undeliberate / chronological defaultThe reader's own assumptions (often 'no news is good news,' or its opposite)

Avoiding a deliberate choice doesn't remove the framing decision — it just hands it to whichever default happens to apply, which is exactly what happened in Draft A.

Common mistake

Treating 'neutral' as a real third option alongside deliberate framing and spin. There is no framing-free narrative — only a deliberate one or an accidental one.

items.learnMore:
Why 'just be chronological' doesn't dodge the choice

Chronological order looks neutral because no one appears to have decided it — but "first we failed, then we fixed it" and "we delivered the result, after a failure we fixed" are both chronological, and they don't read the same.

ChoiceWhat fills the gap
Deliberate framingThe writer's considered judgment about order and emphasis
Undeliberate / chronological defaultThe reader's own assumptions (often 'no news is good news,' or its opposite)

Avoiding a deliberate choice doesn't remove the framing decision — it just hands it to whichever default happens to apply, which is exactly what happened in Draft A.

Treating 'neutral' as a real third option alongside deliberate framing and spin. There is no framing-free narrative — only a deliberate one or an accidental one.

items.prompt: L2 defines materiality using a 'reasonable reader.' Who is that?
choices: A normal person trying to understand the result fairly, not someone looking for excuses to find fault
Only the most senior stakeholder in the room
Whoever is most likely to be upset by bad news
A reader who already knows every operational detail in advance
items.explanation: L2 is specific: the standard is a normal person reading fairly, not an adversarial reader hunting for a technicality, and not an unusually lenient one either — it's a fairness standard, not a worst-case or best-case one.
items.reference:
Reasonable reader
⚖️ A fair reader, not an adversarial one
⚖️ A fair reader, not an unusually lenient one either
Why: materiality is measured against fairness, not against the most suspicious or the most forgiving possible reading.
items.learnMore:
Why the standard is 'reasonable,' not 'any possible'
StandardWhat it would require
Reasonable readerWould a fair reader's understanding of the outcome change?
Any possible readerEvery reader who could conceivably object would have to be satisfied — an impossible bar

Anchoring materiality to a reasonable reader keeps the test workable — a narrative doesn't have to survive the most suspicious imaginable reading, only a fair one.

Common mistake

Defending an omission with 'a sufficiently generous reader wouldn't have minded.' The standard cuts both ways — it also means an omission can't be excused just because some lenient reader wouldn't have cared.

items.learnMore:
Materiality scales with severity, not just presence

The self-check's second question ("is any material fact missing?") has a binary answer. L3's closing question adds a dimension that binary check doesn't capture on its own: a fact can be present and still under-weighted for how serious it is.

OutageHonest treatment

4 hours, affects paying customers directlyNeeds real space: impact, what was fixed, what prevention was added, what remains risky

This is the same instinct as the guiding questions used throughout this unit, applied to a single fact: the question isn't just 'did I mention it,' it's 'did I give it space proportional to what it actually cost.'

Treating the self-check's two yes/no questions as the complete honesty standard. They catch omission and falsehood, but not under-weighting a serious fact that is technically present — that's a third, more judgment-based question the closing section adds.
